article.title: Cloudflare Fixes Cross-Tenant Data Exposure Bug in Containers Within Hours of Bug Bounty Report
article.summary: A researcher found that deleted containers' leftover disk data could leak to other customers; Cloudflare fixed the root cause the same day it was reported.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

Cloudflare has disclosed and fixed a vulnerability in its Containers product that could have let one paying customer recover leftover disk data from other customers' deleted containers running on the same physical server. According to [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/), security researcher Oren Yomtov of Accomplish "responsibly reported" the flaw through Cloudflare's bug bounty program on September 4, 2026, and the company says it "has fully remediated the vulnerability" and has "no evidence that customer data has been compromised."

## What We Know

The issue stemmed from how Cloudflare Containers allocate disk storage. Each container's writable disk is built on Linux's device-mapper thin-provisioning feature, which hands out storage in 64-kilobyte blocks from a pool shared across customers on the same host, according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/cloudflare-fixes-flaw-that-let-one.html). Normally, a block is wiped before it is reassigned to a new container. In this case it wasn't: as [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/) explains, "When such a write reached an unmapped thin block, dm-thin allocated a physical 64 KiB block from the shared pool. The 4 KiB write replaced only that portion of the block, and because block zeroing was disabled, the remaining 60 KiB could retain data from a previous container."

The researchers demonstrated the flaw by writing small four-kilobyte blocks into unused disk space inside a container they controlled, then reading the full 64-kilobyte block back at the raw disk level — recovering the 60 kilobytes they had never written, which still "held bytes from a previous container," per [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/cloudflare-fixes-flaw-that-let-one.html).

Cloudflare says the flaw "would potentially have allowed for a customer with a Workers Paid account to recover residual data from storage blocks previously used by other customers' Containers on the same underlying host," and that the report "affect[ed] Cloudflare Containers and Cloudflare Sandboxes (which is built on Containers)," according to its [own disclosure](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/). The Hacker News adds that Sandboxes "is sold as a safe place to run untrusted code, including code written by AI agents." The researchers separately told The Hacker News that "the same disk setup affected Cloudflare's Browser Run product" too — a claim Cloudflare's own disclosure does not address — and described the finding as "their sixth escape from a code sandbox published since July," according to [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/cloudflare-fixes-flaw-that-let-one.html).

In controlled production testing conducted with Cloudflare's cooperation, the researchers found residual data from other customers at scale. Cloudflare's own account states the researchers "ultimately observed residual material on 18 of 24 placements and 20 of 22 underlying nodes across four continents" — figures that [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/cloudflare-fixes-flaw-that-let-one.html) independently reports in the same terms: "finding leftover material on 18 of 24 tries, each on a server Cloudflare chose, and on 20 of 22 underlying machines across four continents." The data types recovered included "directory listings, SQLite databases, Chromium browser profiles, .env files, and credential files," per [The Hacker News](https://thehackernews.com/2026/09/cloudflare-fixes-flaw-that-let-one.html).

Cloudflare's timeline shows a same-day response: the report landed at 15:26 UTC on September 4, the company confirmed the production flaw by 18:45 UTC, merged a runtime fix by 21:27 UTC, and began rolling it out by 23:15 UTC that same day, according to [Cloudflare](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/). The rollout finished on September 7, and cleanup of cached data created before the mitigation — which required retiring and rebuilding running container disks fleet-wide — completed on September 19. Researchers confirmed their proof-of-concept no longer worked by September 14, and Cloudflare awarded them a bounty that day.

Cloudflare says the fix required no action from customers: it "applied a fix across the Containers fleet, with no customer-side configuration changes required," per its [disclosure](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/). Beyond the initial patch, the company says it "retired all running container disks and removed cached image snapshots created before the mitigation," draining hosts and rebuilding disk caches so that any lingering unzeroed blocks were eliminated fleet-wide.

## What We Don't Know

Cloudflare's investigation of historical disk-I/O telemetry found activity consistent only with the researchers' authorized testing and its own engineers' validation work, and the company states it "saw no evidence that this specific attack vector was exploited by anyone else," according to its [disclosure](https://blog.cloudflare.com/containers-cross-tenant-vulnerability/). Both Cloudflare and The Hacker News note that the technique could not target a specific customer, workload, or host, and that the researchers did not demonstrate any ability to modify another customer's live data or disrupt a running workload — the exposure was read-only and non-targeted. Cloudflare has not disclosed a CVE identifier or a bounty dollar amount for the report, and its own post does not address the researchers' separate claim about Browser Run.
